jwtLogin.title: How credentials turn into a signed token
jwtLogin.description: Login flow: the browser sends credentials, the server checks them against the users table, signs a token and then stores nothing.

steps.credentials: The password leaves the browser exactly once, at login. From here on it never travels again.
steps.verify: The server compares what arrived against the stored hash. This is the only moment in the whole pattern that touches the users table.
steps.sign: With who you are (sub) and how long for (exp), the server builds the payload and seals it with its secret. The signature hides nothing — it guarantees nobody edited it.
steps.deliver: The token goes back to the browser. From now on, whoever holds it is you as far as the server is concerned.
steps.forget: The server keeps no copy. That is why it can validate the token later without looking anything up — and why it cannot switch it off.

jwtValidation.title: What the server does with your token on every request
jwtValidation.description: Validating a JWT: split it in three, recompute the signature, compare the expiry and answer without touching the database.

steps.arrive: The request carries the token in the Authorization header. There is no session cookie to look up anywhere.
steps.split: A token is three parts separated by dots. The first two are base64, so anyone can read the payload: never put a secret in there.
steps.signature: The server recomputes the signature with its secret and compares it to the one in the token. If anyone edited the payload it no longer matches, and that is a 401.
steps.expiry: Then it compares exp against its own clock. An expired token ends in the same 401, however perfect the signature is.
steps.serve: If both checks pass, the sub claim is the identity and the request gets served.
steps.stateless: None of this queried the database. That is the scaling win — and the reason a valid token cannot be switched off.

jwtRefresh.title: Why the pattern needs two tokens, not one
jwtRefresh.description: The refresh cycle: the access token expires, the client trades the refresh token for a fresh pair, and the old one is marked as used.

steps.expired: Fifteen minutes in, the access token expires and the ordinary request comes back with a 401. Nothing broke: this was the plan.
steps.ask: The client does not ask for your password again. It calls /refresh with the refresh token, which travels in a cookie the page's JavaScript cannot read.
steps.lookup: Here there is a lookup. The refresh token lives in a table, and it is the only stateful piece of the pattern.
steps.rotate: The server issues a fresh pair and marks the old one as used. A refresh token is worth exactly one use.
steps.retry: The client retries the original request with the new access token and it goes through. You never noticed a thing.
steps.reuse: If the used refresh token shows up again, somebody has a copy. The answer is to invalidate the whole family and force a login.

jwtLogout.title: Why logging out does not switch the token off
jwtLogout.description: Logging out with JWT: the client drops its token and the server deletes the refresh token, but a copy of the access token keeps passing validation until it expires.

steps.clear: Logging out deletes the token from the browser. That is all the client can do: remove it from its own side.
steps.revoke: The refresh token really is revocable, because it lives in a table. Deleting it closes the door on renewing the session.
steps.copy: But a copy of the access token — in a log, in a proxy, in somebody's clipboard — still carries a correct signature and an exp that has not arrived. The API answers 200.
steps.denylist: The way out is a denylist: you store the revoked token's jti until its exp, and the API checks it before serving.
steps.tradeoff: And there is the state JWT was trying to avoid. You pick: short tokens with a window of minutes, or instant revocation with one read per request.
